The South African shelduck (Tadorna cana) is a striking waterfowl species endemic to southern Africa, where it inhabits both freshwater wetlands and coastal lagoons. Field studies monitoring nesting colonies in the Northern Cape have documented that adult females achieve a maximum asymptotic body mass of approximately 950 grams [Wwi = approximately 950 grams], while males are substantially larger, attaining an ultimate wet weight of about 1200 grams [Wwi = about 1200 grams]. This pronounced sexual size dimorphism is typical of the genus Tadorna and is thought to be linked to the intense male-male competition observed during the breeding season. Newly hatched ducklings emerge from the egg at a surprisingly modest wet weight at birth of around 60 grams [Wwb = around 60 grams], which represents only a small fraction of the adult mass they will eventually reach. This altricial-to-precocial transition is rapid, as the downy chicks are capable of leaving the nest and feeding themselves within a day of hatching, though they remain dependent on parental vigilance for thermoregulation and protection from predators.

Eggs of the South African shelduck require a carefully maintained incubation environment, and controlled laboratory experiments have shown that at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the incubation period leading to hatching lasts approximately 28 days [ab = approximately 28 days]. This age at birth is relatively brief compared to other waterfowl of similar body size, likely reflecting an adaptive strategy to reduce the window of vulnerability during the egg stage in a landscape frequented by mammalian nest predators. Following hatching, the development of the ducklings proceeds under the thermoregulatory conditions typical of the active metabolic phase in this species, which operates at a core body temperature of 41.2 °C [T = 41.2 °C]. The fledging process, defined as the time since birth at fledging when the juvenile achieves independent flight, occurs at roughly 55 days after hatching [tx = roughly 55 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.2 °C [T = 41.2 °C]. This developmental milestone marks the transition from a completely dependent chick to a capable juvenile capable of dispersing from the natal site.

Puberty and the onset of reproductive maturity in the South African shelduck follow a distinct developmental trajectory shaped by seasonal resource availability. At the same thermal regime of 41.2 °C [T = 41.2 °C], which characterizes this species' active metabolic state, the time since birth at puberty has been estimated from gonadal examination of wild specimens as 165 days after hatching [tp = 165 days after hatching]. This relatively rapid progression to sexual maturity is notable among waterfowl, as many larger-bodied waterfowl species delay puberty until their second calendar year. The accelerated maturation in T. cana is likely an adaptation to unpredictable rainfall patterns across their arid and semi-arid range, allowing individuals to exploit brief windows of favorable breeding conditions as soon as they are physically capable. Once puberty is reached, birds undergo a period of further somatic growth and social integration into wintering flocks, where pair bonds for the subsequent breeding season begin to form.

The timing of first successful reproduction in the South African shelduck is a critical life-history parameter that reflects the interplay between physiological readiness and ecological opportunity. Under the metabolic conditions sustained at 41.2 °C [T = 41.2 °C], longitudinal field data indicate that the time since birth at first brood is approximately 2 years after hatching [tR = approximately 2 years after hatching]. This delay between reaching puberty at 165 days and initiating a first brood at two years highlights that social and environmental constraints—such as the acquisition of a suitable nesting burrow and the formation of a stable monogamous pair bond—are more limiting than physiological capacity alone. Furthermore, the maximum lifespan documented for this species in wild populations, drawing on long-term ringing studies, has been reported as 24.8 years [am = 24.8 years] under the same thermal conditions of 41.2 °C [T = 41.2 °C]. Such longevity is substantial for a bird of this size and suggests a life-history strategy characterized by high adult survival and repeated reproductive attempts over a long adult lifespan.

Reproductive output in the South African shelduck is typically expressed in terms of clutch size and the number of nesting attempts per season. Females lay between 6 and 12 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 6 and 12 eggs per clutch], a range that is consistent with values reported for the congeneric ruddy shelduck (Tadorna ferruginea) and indicative of a substantial annual reproductive investment. The number of broods produced annually is typically one [F_R_i = broods produced annually is typically one], reflecting the constraints imposed by the lengthy incubation and chick-rearing periods in a seasonal environment. When combined, this reproductive strategy yields a moderate annual output that is balanced against the high probability of adult survival from one year to the next. The total energetic cost of egg production, incubation, and brood rearing is considerable, and females often enter the post-breeding molt in a depleted body condition, relying on the long post-breeding period to replenish their reserves before the next breeding cycle begins.
